Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette:
Daniel Fischer, a 33-year-old graphic designer, traced the beginning of his problems to a late-night traffic stop that turned violent two years ago. He had been driving home after staying late at the studio, tired and irritated, when flashing lights appeared behind him on a dark stretch of road. He remembered the patrol car pulling up at an angle, the beam of a flashlight cutting through his windshield, and the sudden sense that he could not read what was happening next. When the officers approached with their hands near their weapons and began shouting contradictory commands, he froze. One officer dragged him from the car and forced him to the ground while another kneeled on his back. Daniel recalled the black shape of their uniforms against the road, the metal on their belts, the smell of gasoline, and the humiliation of cars slowing as strangers watched. What stayed with him most was not only the pain but the conviction, formed in those moments on the pavement, that he could be overpowered without warning and that nobody nearby would stop it.

In the months after, the world narrowed in ways that felt logical to him. Nighttime became especially hard. If he woke in the dark, even in his own apartment, he would come up abruptly with his heart racing and a felt sense that someone was there, just outside his vision. Darkness carried him back to the roadside before he had time to remind himself where he was. Similar cars also caught him off guard. A sedan with the same silhouette as the patrol car, especially in his rearview mirror or idling near a curb, could make his body tense before he had consciously registered why. Crowded places were almost as bad. In a packed grocery line or on a busy sidewalk, he felt trapped in the same way he had on the ground with people around him and no room to move.

Those moments shaped what he did to get through the day. Daniel started drinking in the evenings because it was the quickest way he knew to blunt what nighttime did to him; if he could get himself foggy enough before bed, he thought he might sleep through the dark rather than wake into it. On especially difficult nights he mixed alcohol with whatever medication he had on hand, less out of recklessness than desperation to make himself unconscious. When he had to go out, he became vigilant about avoiding police officers, security guards, or anyone in uniform, crossing streets or leaving stores if he saw a weapon on a belt. In crowded places, particularly if he felt suddenly exposed, he would lift his hands to his face as if rubbing his eyes or adjusting his glasses, but really to block out what was around him and hide himself for a few seconds until the surge passed. The same thing happened if a car resembling the patrol vehicle rolled by while he was walking; his hands came up before he had thought it through.

His work as a graphic designer had made these habits harder to contain. The agency where he worked occupied an open-plan office downtown, and client meetings often meant walking through dense lunchtime crowds or staying late and driving home after dark. He began finding reasons to work remotely, claiming he needed uninterrupted time for deadlines, though privately he was trying to avoid the commute home at night and the streets around the courthouse where police cars were regularly parked. When he did go in, he timed his breaks to avoid the busiest elevator periods and sometimes took the stairs just to escape the feeling of being hemmed in. Colleagues noticed he was less available and more erratic with deadlines. After one evening presentation, he went straight home, drank heavily, and missed the next morning's review. His divorce had already left him living alone, and over time there was no one in the apartment to interrupt the pattern of drinking, sleeping badly, and waking in darkness with his pulse pounding.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was frightened by how automatic his life had become. He could see that whole routes through the city, whole hours of the day, and whole categories of people had been marked off as dangerous. He was drinking most nights and ashamed of how often his first impulse in public was to hide his face like he was still on the ground trying to disappear. What finally brought him in was a recent episode after leaving work late: a police cruiser was parked across from his building, and he turned around, walked three extra blocks to avoid passing it, then went home and drank until he blacked out. He said he was scared that if this kept going, he would lose his job. More quietly, he admitted that what he wanted most was to be able to wake up in the dark and know, immediately and fully, that he was safe.
